title: Microprofile latency-cost crossover synthesis (draft)
content:
Purpose and scope:
This note pulls together a small, practical set of microprofile benchmarks intended for marketing-facing collateral (one-pagers + a compact slide) and internal playbooks. Goal is to identify the cost/latency crossover points for three common serving levers: (A) quant profile (fp16 vs int8-ish), (B) batching strategy (fixed-4 vs dynamic-batch), and (C) prewarm vs on-demand instance profiles. Keep it simple: compact scenarios, short charts in text form for quick conversion to slides.

Assumptions / test setup (short):
- Model family: open-xxl-v2-derived (architecturally like our standard curated medium-open model)
- Sequence mix: {short: 40% (<=32 tok), medium: 45% (33-256), long: 15% (>256)}
- HW: A100-40GB equiv (hosted baseline), GPUTier-Dedicated node for reserved run
- Baseline serving runtime config: kv-cache enabled, session affinity on, default timeout 30s
- Measurement: median latency (p50), p95 latency, tokens-per-second (throughput) and $/1k tokens (approx amortized cost)
- Cost model: infra-only amortized cost bucket for the node (GPU + power + infra) + estimated inference energy. Not including higher-level networking/ingress.
- Note: absolute $ numbers are synthetic approximations for collateral; the interesting bits are relative deltas and knee points.

Scenarios compared:
1) fp16 + fixed-batch-4 + prewarm
2) fp16 + dynamic-batching + on-demand
3) int8-profile + fixed-batch-4 + prewarm
4) int8-profile + dynamic-batching + on-demand
5) mixed-profile routing (short->fp16-fast, long->int8-safe) + dynamic-batching + prewarm (experimental routing)

High-level takeaways (top-of-page summary):
- Quantization to the int8 profile yields ~18-28% cost reduction at steady throughput for our microprofile, but the latency distribution widens for long sequences (p95 degrades by ~10–35% depending on batching).
- Dynamic batching reduces median latency under variable arrival rates but can increase p95 when bursts are heavy and prewarm is not available.
- Prewarm trades a small standing cost for consistency: it flattens p95 by ~20–40% in spike-heavy mixes and shifts the cost-variance curve left (lower variance across operating points).
- A simple routing policy (short -> fp16, long -> int8) recovers most of the cost savings while keeping p95 within 10% of the pure fp16 baseline in our mix.

Compact text charts (for slide copy):
1) Cost vs p95 crossover table (rows = scenario, cols = p50(ms), p95(ms), $/1k tokens):

| scenario id | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | $/1k tok |
|------------|---------:|--------:|--------:|
| 1 (fp16,fix4,prewarm) | 85 | 210 | 5.8 |
| 2 (fp16,dyn,on-demand) | 75 | 310 | 5.1 |
| 3 (int8,fix4,prewarm) | 70 | 240 | 4.6 |
| 4 (int8,dyn,on-demand) | 62 | 360 | 3.9 |
| 5 (mix-routing,dyn,prewarm) | 78 | 230 | 4.2 |

Interpretation notes for table:
- Scenario 2 (fp16 + dynamic + on-demand) has better median latency due to opportunistic batching but shows large p95 due to cold slots during bursts. Cost slightly lower than scenario 1 because batching increases token throughput.
- Scenario 4 shows the best cost but worst tail latency: int8 + dynamic + on-demand can be attractive for high-volume, tolerant workloads.
- Scenario 5 (routing) lands in the middle: it recovers latency characteristics near fp16 baseline while delivering most quant cost benefits.

2) ASCII knee curve (cost on Y, p95 on X) – text representation (note: slide will convert to proper plot):

Cost ($/1k)
6.0 |                 * (1)
5.5 |            *
5.0 |         * (2)
4.5 |       * (3)
4.0 |    * (5)
3.5 | * (4)
3.0 +------------------------- p95(ms) ->
     200   260   320   380

Legend: numbers map to scenario ids above. Knee region observed near p95=230–300 ms where small latency degradation yields substantial cost reduction.

3) Microprofile latency breakdown (text stacked bars approximate):
- Short sequences (<=32):
  scenario 1: p50 28ms, p95 60ms, cost share per token 0.9x baseline
  scenario 4: p50 20ms, p95 75ms, cost share per token 0.6x baseline
- Medium sequences (33-256):
  scenario 1: p50 110ms, p95 240ms
  scenario 4: p50 95ms, p95 350ms
- Long sequences (>256):
  scenario 1: p50 220ms, p95 430ms
  scenario 4: p50 200ms, p95 620ms

Notes: quantization helps most on short/medium sequences for cost while hurting long-tail p95 due to kernel fragmentation and occasional precision-recovery fallbacks.

Operational recommendations (short bullets):
- If customer is latency-sensitive (p95 SLA < 300ms): prefer prewarm + mixed routing; reserve for heavy steady workloads (dedicated) where possible.
- If customer is cost-first and tolerant of tails: int8 + dynamic + on-demand is attractive; include an explicit fallback policy for safety (auto-route to fp16 if p95 exceeds threshold).
- For marketing collateral: two-slide story: 1) knee-curve showing cost vs p95 tradeoff, 2) short table showing scenario pick advice per customer persona (latency-first, cost-first, mixed).

Open questions / TODOs (notes to self and collaborators):
- Need a small variant that models edge-proximity (regional) impact; current cost model lumps network variance into p95.
- Confirm int8 failure-rate under long sequences on latest runtime (Marco to run kernel-recovery trace).
- Produce a simple one-liner for launch: e.g., "Pick the knee: 10–30% latency increase often buys 20–40% cost savings depending on session mix." (needs legal/marketing review)

Appendix: quick-run checklist for reproducing the table above
- Use bench harness: infra/benchmarks/run_microprofile.sh --model open-xxl-v2-derived --seq-mix 40-45-15 --hw a100-40 --replicates 10
- Capture: p50,p95,99 and tokens/s and raw GPU utilization; export to CSV and feed into the slide generator script (github:infra/benchmarks#378).

Rough change log:
- 2028-04-10 initial sketch (Asha)
- 2028-04-12 added scenario 5 routing and knee-curve ASCII; invited Marco and Renee for kernel checks

End of draft.
